instances.label: Console/remote fault: a monitoring alert or escalated ticket (service crashed, authentication failures, DNS/DHCP/VPN misconfiguration, full volume, failed backup job, patch regression, slow application). The admin works from a workstation in an office or NOC using SSH/RDP, management consoles, logs and packet captures; no hardware is touched; the fix is a configuration change, restart, rollback, or script.

Physical-layer link fault in a structured cabling / patch field (data center MDF, carrier meet-me room, campus fiber plant): a circuit is down or lossy; the admin tests the path (light levels, OTDR, loopback), isolates the bad cord, transceiver or cross-connect, and re-patches or replaces the connection to restore service.

On-site replacement of failed network gear in employer-controlled buildings and branch sites: a dead access switch, PoE injector, ceiling-mounted access point, branch router or firewall. The admin travels to the closet/ceiling/branch, confirms the fault (LEDs, console cable, power test), unmounts or unracks the unit, installs the spare, re-cables it, restores config and verifies traffic.

End-user device hardware fault: a laptop or desktop that won't boot or has a failing SSD, RAM stick, battery, GPU, dock, cable, or a jammed/failed printer. Diagnosis at a cluttered user desk or on an IT workshop bench; disassemble, isolate the bad part by swap-testing, install the replacement, reassemble and verify the machine works.

Racked-server drive failure in a server room or data center: an array/storage-node alert identifies a failed disk; the admin locates the rack, machine and bay, pulls the failed hot-swap drive, inserts the replacement, and verifies the rebuild completes.

In-chassis server or appliance repair: replace a DIMM, power supply, fan module, RAID controller or NIC, or swap out and re-cable a whole failed server/appliance (RMA) in the rack, then reinstall firmware/config and return it to service.

sources.title: The slow rise of robots in the data center - DCD
sources.claim: Alibaba Cloud's second-generation Tianxun robot performs inspection, locates a faulty hard disk and replaces it in a production data center without human intervention, in about four minutes; claimed in operation at five Alibaba data centers.

sources.claim: Independent trade-press corroboration that Alibaba Cloud operates robots that find and replace faulty disks in its data centers in four minutes (video showed a 3.5-inch SAS/SATA drive being handled).

sources.system: Telescent G4/G5 Network Topology Manager (robotic patch panel)
sources.developer: Telescent Inc. (deployed by MOX Networks, Quantum Loophole and others)
sources.title: MOX Signs Agreement to Deploy Telescent's Fiber Automation Platform on its Next-Generation Long-Haul Route
sources.claim: Telescent's G4/G5 Network Topology Manager is a commercially deployed robotic fiber patch panel that makes, tests and reconfigures physical fiber connections under software control, supporting remote fault isolation and service restoration without dispatching a technician.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated physical-layer provisioning/testing. It transfers to physical-layer fault resolution because the same robot locates cable faults and re-patches the defective connection - the same objects (LC fiber cords), the same sub-millimeter insertion precision, and the same facility.

sources.system: Patchy McPatchbot and successor patch robots (X-Y gantry fiber patching)
sources.title: DE-CIX migrates Frankfurt data center without disruption using patch robot - DCD
sources.claim: DE-CIX has run automated patch robots at its Frankfurt internet exchange since 2018; the robots plug fiber cords into an optical distribution frame built for them and independently migrated live customer connections during a data center move.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic fiber patching in a live exchange. It bears on resolving physical-layer faults because restoring or re-routing a defective connection is the same manipulation, but only inside a purpose-built optical distribution frame rather than a hand-dressed patch panel.

sources.title: Google tests robots for managing data center hard drives and equipment - DCD
sources.claim: As of the October 2024 OCP Global Summit, Google was still testing robots for handling hard drives and equipment in its data centers, citing interest in rack movement, servicing and media management - i.e., general robotic servicing of racked IT equipment is not yet in worker-quality production use at hyperscalers.
sources.transferJustification: Bounding evidence for the same task family (robotic servicing of racked IT hardware): it shows the state of the art at hyperscale is test deployments for media handling, not diagnose-and-repair of arbitrary components.

sources.system: Daisy (with Dave and Taz) disassembly robots
sources.title: Meet Daisy and Taz: Apple's iPhone-Disassembling Robots | Supply Chain Digital
sources.claim: Apple's Daisy robot autonomously disassembles 23 iPhone models at 200 units per hour on a purpose-built line, separating components for material recovery - automated teardown of consumer electronics, but not fault diagnosis, part replacement, reassembly or functional verification.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic disassembly of electronic devices, the closest automated analogue to opening a laptop or server to reach a defective part. It covers only teardown of known models on a fixtured line for recycling, so it does not substantiate diagnose-replace-reassemble-verify repair.

sources.system: Automated electronics disassembly research cell (Fraunhofer IFF)
sources.developer: Fraunhofer Institute for Factory Operation and Automation IFF
sources.title: Automated Electronics Disassembly: First Milestones in the Research Project - Fraunhofer IFF
sources.claim: Fraunhofer IFF research demonstrated automated disassembly subprocesses on electronics including tool selection, unscrewing and removing a computer motherboard, still at research-project milestone stage in 2025 and dependent on known components in defined condition.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic teardown of PCs/servers in a fixtured cell. It is the nearest evidence for in-chassis component work, but it removes parts from known devices for recycling and does not diagnose faults or restore a working machine.

tasks.label: Maintain an inventory of parts for emergency repairs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Periodic stock check of the spare-parts cabinet/shelf in the server room or IT closet: loose, mixed items (drives in ESD bags, SFP transceivers, patch cables, RAM, fans, PSUs, a cold-spare switch), many in opened or unlabeled boxes; count, verify model/serial, reconcile against a spreadsheet or CMDB, flag shortfalls.

Cycle count/audit in a larger enterprise or data-center stockroom where spares are barcode- or RFID-tagged and shelved in labeled bins along walkable aisles; robot-readable identifiers exist; count, reconcile with the asset system, report discrepancies and low stock.

Receiving spares: unpack vendor cartons and RMA replacement shipments, check part numbers/serials against the packing slip, apply asset/inventory tags, put each item away in the correct bin or shelf location, and update the inventory record.

Emergency pull during an incident: locate and retrieve the correct spare (matching drive model, transceiver, power supply, patch cable) from the stockroom bin, carry it to the rack/data-center floor, then decrement stock and open a reorder/RMA to replenish.

Housekeeping/purge: review the spares hoard, decide what is obsolete (parts for decommissioned platforms, expired UPS batteries, dead RMA cores), pull and stage them for e-waste or vendor core return, break down boxes, relabel and reorganize bins, and update records.

Branch/remote-site spares: check and restock small caches kept at branch offices, remote wiring closets or colo cages during site visits; pack and ship parts between sites; verify depot/vendor stock levels for the remote locations.

sources.system: AutoCrib RoboCrib VX1000 / TX750 industrial vending systems

sources.system: Kardex Shuttle Vertical Lift Module (spare parts management)
sources.title: Automated Spare Parts Management & Inventory Control | Kardex
sources.claim: Kardex sells vertical lift modules purpose-built for spare-parts management, storing high SKU counts and retrieving them automatically for MRO use.

sources.title: AutoStore Automated Storage and Retrieval System | Dematic
sources.claim: AutoStore is a widely deployed bin-grid ASRS in which autonomous robots store and retrieve inventory bins and present them at ports, with ~99.8% system availability.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated storage/retrieval of small-part inventory. Provides the purpose-built environment in which stock levels are inherently tracked and parts are presented to a picking machine.

sources.system: eOperator robotic piece-picking cell (RightPick) on AutoStore
sources.title: Robotic arm connected to AutoStore at Solar - Element Logic
sources.claim: Element Logic's eOperator (RightHand Robotics RightPick technology) runs in production at Solar A/S, an electrical and technical components distributor, autonomously piece-picking items from AutoStore ports into outgoing packages.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic each-picking of electrical/technical components from storage bins. Objects (connectors, cables, small electronic components) and precision are comparable to network spare parts; it closes the loop from stored stock to issued part.

sources.title: Introducing Vulcan: Amazon's first robot with a sense of touch
sources.claim: Amazon's Vulcan robot autonomously picks and stows individual items into inventory pods in live fulfillment centers in Spokane and Hamburg, handling roughly three-quarters of the ~1 million item types stocked there.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: put-away (stow) of heterogeneous small items into storage bins and retrieval of specific items. Same physical operation as shelving received spares and pulling one back out, with pods presented to the machine.

sources.title: How Diligent's Robots Are Making a Difference in Texas Hospitals - IEEE Spectrum
sources.claim: Diligent Robotics' Moxi mobile manipulator autonomously picks known supplies out of hospital supply closets and delivers them, using per-room taught visual cues and bins in rooms also used by staff.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fetching a specified stocked item from a shared institutional supply room and delivering it. Object class (boxed/bagged consumables in labeled bins), precision, and indoor institution-controlled setting match an IT stockroom pull.

sources.title: Improving operations and product availability at stores globally (IFR case study)
sources.claim: PAL Robotics' StockBot, an autonomous RFID mobile robot, is deployed at Decathlon stores to automate stock counting that staff previously did manually and error-prone.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous cycle counting of tagged stock in an institution-run facility. Reading tagged items on shelves and reconciling counts with the inventory system is the same operation as auditing a tagged IT stockroom.

sources.title: Fetch Autonomous Mobile Robots | Zetes
sources.claim: Zebra's Fetch TagSurveyor AMR performs autonomous inventory cycle counting by collecting and locating RFID tags on products and ... inside warehouses and factories.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic cycle counting of tagged parts in bins inside a human-run facility; identical operation to auditing an RFID-tagged spares stockroom and reporting discrepancies.

sources.title: Simbe's Tally Inventory Robot Deployed in Harmons Stores Following Pilot Success
sources.claim: Simbe's Tally autonomous shelf-scanning robot is deployed across 17 Harmons grocery stores, capturing shelf-level availability data that staff previously verified by hand.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous shelf inventory audit in an institution-controlled facility; supports counting/reconciling labeled, shelved stock, though it addresses front-faced packaged goods rather than loose parts in bins.

instances.label: Server room / data center: load and rotate LTO backup tapes — insert cartridges into a standalone drive, autoloader or library I/O station, remove and barcode-label completed tapes, box them for offsite rotation, verify the job mounted.

Server room: insert or replace storage disks in racked servers and arrays — pull a hot-swap drive caddy, seat a replacement 2.5"/3.5" drive or NVMe/SSD in the correct bay, confirm the array rebuilds; also seat removable media in an appliance.

Office or server room: install OS/software at the machine's console from physical media — carry a USB stick or DVD to a server/workstation, insert it, boot, and drive the installer through to a working system.

Office: refill copier/MFP and laser printer paper trays and load special stock — pre-printed forms, check stock, label sheets, multi-part forms — squaring the ream, setting tray guides, clearing a misfeed.

Branch office back room, warehouse office, wiring closet, or a remote employee's home office: same media/paper/forms loading in a cluttered, non-standard space with equipment wherever it happens to sit.

sources.system: HIL-SERL (human-in-the-loop RL manipulation policies on Franka arms)
sources.title: Precise and Dexterous Robotic Manipulation via Human-in-the-Loop Reinforcement Learning
sources.claim: A learned policy on a fixtured bench performs RAM insertion, SSD assembly and USB grasp-and-insertion at 100% success after 1-2.5 hours of training, then executes autonomously.
sources.transferJustification: Related tasks: RAM/SSD seating and USB plug insertion. These are the same physical acts as seating a hot-swap drive or inserting install media — rigid computer components, sub-millimetre slot tolerances, on a fixtured bench equivalent to a purpose-built cell.

sources.system: Epson Discproducer PP-100III / PP-50II (AcuGrip robotic arm)
sources.title: Epson Discproducer PP-100III CD/DVD/Blu-ray Disc Publisher | Media Supply
sources.claim: Commercial desktop disc publishers use a robotic arm to pick single blank discs and load them into optical drives and a printer for unattended production runs.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: loading optical discs into a drive. This is the same act as loading a software/OS disc into a machine's drive — same media geometry, same tray/slot insertion tolerance — performed unattended in a purpose-built enclosure.

sources.title: The Rise of Robotics: Automating Wide Format Print Production - FESPA
sources.claim: Durst's P5 Robotics uses two KUKA arms with a registration station to pick print media from a stack and place it accurately on the printer, automating loading of a wide-format press.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: loading print media into a printer. Same objects (sheets/stock taken from a stack), same requirement of accurate registration into the printer's feed position; substantiates robotic paper/forms loading in a purpose-built print cell.

sources.title: The Robotic Material Handler - Kongsberg Precision Cutting Systems
sources.claim: A commercial robotic sheet handler loads and unloads print media directly from pallets with high precision and keeps a printing/finishing machine fed through an entire unattended shift.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: feeding paper/board stock into a printing/cutting machine from a stack. Comparable objects (paper stock), comparable placement precision, and it must keep the machine supplied unattended — the same output as refilling a printer's paper supply.

sources.title: Patchy McPatchbot helps DE-CIX move 450 customers to new data centre | Capacity Media
sources.claim: DE-CIX operates 'patch robots' that independently plug and reconnect fiber connections on an optical distribution frame in a live data center, used to migrate 450+ customers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: precise connector insertion into rack-mounted IT equipment. Shows machine-controlled insertion of small connectors at production quality, but only into a frame purpose-built for the robot, not into ordinary human-built racks.

sources.title: OCP 2024 Spotlight: Meta Debuts 140 kW Liquid-Cooled AI Rack; Google Eyes Robotics to Muscle Hyperscaler GPUs | Data Center Frontier
sources.claim: Google showed video at OCP 2024 of large robots moving through a data center managing hard drives ...; described as testing rather than production service.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: handling drives inside a data center. Corroborates the Alibaba deployment direction, but autonomy is not established, so it is treated as non-supporting.

instances.label: Physical security walkthrough of a client enterprise or colocation data hall as part of an assessment engagement: tester tours aisles, tries cabinet/cage doors and rack locks, looks for exposed console and USB ports, unlabeled patch cabling and unsecured spare gear, checks entry controls (mantrap, badge readers, camera coverage), fire suppression, leak detection under raised floor, UPS/generator siting, and environmental sensor/alarm coverage, then writes risk-rated findings.

Environmental/thermal survey of a client's data hall or server room to identify exposure to overheating: walk the hot and cold aisles capturing rack inlet temperatures and infrared images of racks, PDUs and cooling units, map hot spots against ASHRAE/SLA thresholds, and deliver a hot-spot map and list of at-risk equipment.

Corporate office, branch or retail site review of server closets, IDF/wiring closets and unattended network gear: closets shared with cleaning supplies and stock, cluttered and often warm; tester checks closet and rack locks, exposed switches/APs/cameras/console ports, signs of inadequate cooling (portable fans, no vents), overhead water pipes, and tamper/vandalism exposure from staff, cleaners and visitors.

Physical red-team intrusion test: approach the site from the street/parking lot, probe fence lines, doors, windows and loading docks, attempt tailgating, badge cloning, under-door and lock bypass, reach the server room or comms room, and demonstrate ability to steal, damage or plant a device on servers or network gear; document the path and defeats.

Remote/edge infrastructure assessment: outdoor telecom or ISP cabinets, cell-site shelters, rooftop and pole-mounted gear, remote branch back rooms and industrial/utility control cabinets — inspect for heat build-up, weather and flood exposure, corrosion, prior vandalism or forced-entry damage, and adequacy of enclosures, anchoring and locks.

instances.label: Forensic lab: analyst takes a seized desktop/laptop out of evidence packaging, removes the internal HDD/SSD (or uses a write-blocked adapter/Target Disk Mode), attaches it to a hardware imager or workstation, creates an E01/raw forensic image, verifies source and image hashes, labels the target and updates chain-of-custody records.

Forensic lab: mobile device acquisition — analyst selects the correct cable/profile, connects a seized phone or tablet to Cellebrite UFED/GrayKey/Oxygen, works through device screens (unlock, USB debugging, trust prompts), runs logical/full-file-system/physical extraction, verifies and exports the extraction package.

Forensic lab: loose media — a bag of USB flash drives, SD cards, optical discs and external drives from one seizure; each is inserted into a write-blocked reader/duplicator, imaged individually, hash-verified, labeled and logged.

On-scene acquisition at a residence, small business or client site during a search warrant or incident response: live RAM capture and disk imaging of running machines found as-is, under varied layouts, cabling and power conditions, with time and access constraints.

Remote/network/cloud acquisition from the analyst's office workstation: deploying an EDR/IR agent to collect triage, memory and disk images over the network, or copying VM snapshots and cloud-account exports; no physical media is handled.

Forensic lab: producing working/archive copies — duplicating an existing forensic image file to analysis storage, restoring an image onto a target drive for boot testing, and swapping target drives or writing archive media, with hash re-verification.

tasks.label: Preserve and maintain digital forensic evidence for analysis.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Enterprise/consulting incident response: from a workstation in an office or SOC, the analyst preserves evidence remotely — agent-based triage packages, memory and logical disk images pulled from live endpoints, plus cloud/SaaS and network log exports — hashing each collection, writing it to the case evidence share with acquisition metadata, and verifying integrity. No physical handling of media.

Forensic lab acquisition from a seized computer or loose drive: analyst unseals and photographs the item, removes the drive (or uses a write-blocked live/boot acquisition), creates an E01/raw image on a hardware imager or workstation, verifies MD5/SHA hashes, records chain of custody, then reseals the exhibit and returns it to the evidence locker. Heterogeneous makes/models arrive in evidence bags.

Mobile device preservation, routine case: a modern smartphone arrives (Faraday bag, passcode known or device unlocked); analyst isolates it, connects the correct USB cable to a UFED/GrayKey-class extraction unit, accepts on-screen trust/USB-debugging prompts, runs a logical or full-file-system extraction, hashes and exports the container, and documents the acquisition.

Non-routine device preservation: locked, damaged, legacy or unusual exhibits (feature phones, drones, vehicle infotainment, DVRs, IoT boards, loose flash chips) requiring device-specific teardown, adapter/jig selection, ISP/JTAG connection or chip-off desoldering, and bespoke methods to obtain and verify an image without altering data.

On-scene collection at a residence, small business or vehicle: triage running systems, capture volatile memory, decide what to seize, photograph and label devices, place phones in Faraday bags, seal and tag exhibits, and transport them under chain of custody to the lab.

Maintaining the evidence store: periodic hash re-verification of archived case images, backing up and migrating images to NAS and LTO tape archive, applying retention schedules and secure disposal of expired media, and auditing evidence-locker/media inventory against the case management system.

instances.label: Law-enforcement lab intake: analyst receives seized phones, laptops and drives, verifies the search warrant/consent scope covers the items, completes and signs chain-of-custody documentation, and records the items in the evidence management system before any examination begins. The adherence output is the authorization check plus the custody record, not the carrying of the box.

Acquisition and examination under SOP: analyst confirms the required legal and procedural steps for the exam — write-protection policy, hash verification and documentation, validated-tool requirements, keeping search terms and artifacts within the authorized scope, flagging privileged or out-of-scope material to counsel, and logging every action in the case notes.

Corporate/IR and e-discovery setting: analyst applies legal hold, data-privacy (e.g., GDPR/state privacy law), employee-monitoring and cross-border transfer policies before collecting from employee endpoints, cloud tenants or BYOD devices; obtains written authorization from legal counsel and documents the basis for each collection.

Retention, disposition and audit: analyst follows policy on secure storage duration, sealed-container handling, media sanitization or return/destruction at case closure, and produces records for internal audit or ISO 17025 / accreditation review of media-handling practice.

Currency and testimony: analyst completes periodic legal/compliance training, tracks changes in case law, statutes and agency policy affecting digital media handling, updates or acknowledges revised SOPs, and defends the compliance of the handling process in reports, depositions or courtroom testimony.

instances.label: Enterprise incident response: analyst remotely triages and acquires forensic images (disk/logical collections plus memory) from compromised endpoints across a corporate network using deployed agents (e.g., EDR, Velociraptor/KAPE, F-Response), writing images to a collection server, hashing them and recording chain of custody — performed entirely from a workstation over the network.

Cloud and virtualized environments: preserving evidence by taking volume/VM snapshots and exporting disk images (e.g., EBS snapshot, VMDK export), and capturing network configuration artifacts (VPC/flow-log settings, security groups, firewall and load-balancer configs) through consoles and APIs.

Live capture of volatile state and network settings on running hosts and network gear: running interface/route/ARP/netstat and DNS/DHCP queries, exporting router, switch and firewall running-configs, and capturing packet traces, then hashing and documenting the collected output as evidence.

Law-enforcement or corporate lab imaging of a seized computer: analyst removes the storage device (or uses the machine's interface), connects it through a hardware write blocker or forensic duplicator (e.g., Tableau, Falcon-NEO), starts a bit-for-bit acquisition, verifies MD5/SHA hashes, and completes acquisition documentation; media vary (SATA, NVMe, laptop teardown, soldered storage).

Mobile device acquisition: cabling a phone or tablet to a Cellebrite/GrayKey-type extraction platform, selecting the appropriate logical/file-system/physical method, running the extraction and verifying hashes; occasionally requiring disassembly, ISP or chip-off handling.

On-scene/field acquisition at a business or residence: live-imaging a running server or workstation that cannot be powered off, capturing network settings and volatile data first, writing to a portable target drive or duplicator, under time pressure and in uncontrolled surroundings.

instances.label: Lab workstation: analyst mounts a forensic image (E01/dd) of a seized computer hard drive in a forensic suite (EnCase, X-Ways, Autopsy), runs file carving and unallocated-space recovery to restore deleted documents, images and database fragments, and validates hashes for the case file.

Seized locked smartphone connected by cable to a Cellebrite/GrayKey-type extraction workstation: analyst selects the exploit/profile, runs brute-force or full-file-system extraction, and decrypts the resulting container to produce a readable dataset. The physical act is plugging in a cable; the output is data.

Encrypted volume or container (BitLocker, VeraCrypt, encrypted archive, password-protected office files) from an imaged drive: analyst builds targeted wordlists/rules and runs distributed GPU password cracking (hashcat) or applies recovered keys from memory dumps, then mounts and exports the plaintext.

Cloud/network-side recovery: with legal process, analyst pulls account backups, mail stores or server snapshots, decrypts backup archives with obtained keys, and reconstructs deleted or partially overwritten records — done entirely over network connections from the analyst's workstation.

Physically damaged or failing media (burned/water-damaged drive, dead SSD controller, soldered eMMC/NAND): analyst performs or coordinates bench-level work — PCB/head repair in a clean room, JTAG/ISP hookup, or chip-off desoldering and reading — then reassembles and decrypts the raw image. Usually escalated to a specialist lab.

Physical install of new server, storage or network hardware into racks in a data center/server room: unboxing, mounting rails and chassis, connecting power and network/fiber cabling, labeling, cable management, power-on and firmware/BIOS verification.

Internal component upgrade requiring chassis service: adding or replacing DIMMs, PCIe/NIC/GPU cards, CPUs and heatsinks, internal drives or cables; the machine is powered down and often taken to a bench or staging area in the server room, then reinstalled and validated.

End-user workstation and lab equipment maintenance in offices: installing or swapping desktops/laptops, docks, monitors, memory or SSD upgrades at users' desks or lab benches, plus imaging and software installs on the machine.

Field/edge site work: branch offices, wiring closets, factory floors and remote cabinets where layout varies site to site; mount and cable a switch, firewall or edge appliance, upgrade its firmware/software, and verify connectivity on site.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: physical-layer cabling moves/adds/changes, a routine part of hardware maintenance. sources.title: IBM TS4500 Tape Library
sources.claim: IBM's TS4500 enterprise tape library uses dual robotic accessors that autonomously fetch, insert and remove cartridges into drive slots inside a data-center machine; a mature commercial product line.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated handling of storage media modules. It substantiates that when slots and modules are presented in fixed, known positions (a purpose-built setting), robots insert and extract rack-slot hardware reliably at production quality.

sources.system: Robotic DIMM insertion cells in electronics manufacturing (Google technical disclosure describing the practice and an insertion-girdle fix)

sources.transferJustification: Related task: installing memory modules into motherboards is the same physical operation as a server or workstation memory upgrade, and it is performed by robots where the board is fixtured - exactly the E1 counterfactual presentation.

instances.label: Periodic (bi-weekly/monthly) construction-administration walk of a large BIM-modeled commercial or institutional project mid-construction: traverse multiple floors of an active jobsite, compare installed structure, slabs, partitions and MEP rough-in against the drawings/model, photograph and record conditions, and issue a field report flagging work not in accordance with the documents.

Site visit on a small project - single-family residence, renovation, or small commercial/tenant work - typically documented in 2D drawings with no BIM: ad hoc site with debris, ladders or temporary stairs, partial floors; architect verifies framing layout, rough openings, ceiling heights, beam/header sizes and materials against the plans.

Finishes-phase and punch-list walkthrough near substantial completion: judge workmanship and conformance of finishes (tile layout, paint, drywall, millwork, hardware, alignment, damage, specified colors/products), operate doors and hardware, and compile a deficiency list for correction.

Targeted observation of details and concealed conditions, usually before cover-up: flashing and waterproofing laps, air/vapor barriers, fire-stopping, insulation, blocking, anchorage, correct specified products; includes reviewing mock-ups and walking the condition with the contractor to resolve field questions.

Exterior and sitework observation: excavation, footings and foundations, grading and drainage against the site plan, plus facade and roofing progress observed outdoors in weather, on uneven or muddy terrain and at height.

instances.label: Vacant suburban or rural lot for a single-family house or small building: architect walks the parcel (often with the client), observes topography, trees, drainage patterns, soil surface, sun/views, road access, well/septic or utility feasibility, neighboring structures; takes photos and rough measurements, then issues a go/no-go opinion with siting constraints.

Urban or suburban infill parcel in a built-up block, sometimes with a structure to be demolished or reused: architect assesses party walls and adjacent buildings, alley/sidewalk and staging access, easements, curb cuts, visible utility connections, overhead lines, condition of any existing structure, and reports whether the site can accommodate the proposed program.

Proposed addition or new building on an institution-controlled site (school, hospital, corporate or university campus, occupied office building): architect tours interior and exterior areas with facilities staff, verifies as-built conditions against drawings, checks structural/mechanical capacity, code and accessibility barriers, and judges suitability of the proposed location.

Multi-acre greenfield or brownfield development parcel for a commercial/institutional project: architect walks the site with civil engineer, geotech and developer, reviews grading and stormwater, evidence of wetlands or floodplain, road access, easements, utility stubs, adjacent uses and nuisances, and contributes a suitability/feasibility assessment.

Difficult or hazardous site: steep hillside, heavily wooded acreage, debris-strewn industrial brownfield or fire/storm-damaged lot; rough footing, dense vegetation, unknown hazards; architect makes a limited visual reconnaissance and judges buildability and what further investigation is required.

Substantial-completion / punch-list walkthrough of a finished park, campus quad or streetscape: itemizing deficiencies (dead or declining plants, wrong species or size, mulch depth, staking, settlement, chipped pavers, edging), photographing each, producing a punch list and reviewing it with client and contractor.

Inspection of delivered materials and installed hardscape details on site: comparing soil mix, aggregate base, mulch, stone/pavers and site furnishings against approved submittals; checking base depth, joint widths, setting bed, edge restraint and workmanship; advising the crew on corrections.

Warranty / plant-establishment inspection roughly a year after installation at a park or campus landscape: assessing plant survival and health plant by plant, diagnosing causes (irrigation, drainage, staking, maintenance), testing irrigation operation, and reporting required replacements to the client.

instances.label: At a digital photogrammetric workstation (e.g., Socet GXP, ImageStation, SUMMIT Evolution) in an office, the photogrammetrist views a stereo model of aerial imagery with 3D glasses and a stereo cursor, and digitizes planimetric cultural features — building footprints, road edges, driveways, fences, utility structures — into a CAD/GIS vector file for a municipal basemap.

Compiling terrain: floating the stereo cursor on the ground surface to collect breaklines, spot elevations, and contours for a topographic map or DTM from stereo aerial photography, then editing the contours for cadence and consistency against the model.

Delineating hydrography — stream centerlines, shorelines, drainage ditches, wetland edges, culvert inlets — from stereo imagery, applying agency specifications (e.g., NHD or USGS standards) for feature coding and connectivity.

Identifying, marking, and measuring photo-identifiable control points and pass/tie points in stereo models during aerotriangulation setup, annotating point locations against surveyed control descriptions and photo-control diagrams.

QC/edit pass: reviewing another compiler's delineated features in stereo, correcting misplaced lines, missed features, elevation busts, and edge-match errors between adjoining models or tiles before delivery.

Legacy or specialty work: manual delineation with drafting instruments, ink/scribe on stable-base film or mylar overlays, or annotating hardcopy photo mosaics and orthophoto prints for a client, historical map reproduction, or a courtroom/legal exhibit.

Land-cover/vegetation ground truthing over rural land: travel across forest, farmland and wetland to sample locations, identify and record cover class and stand attributes, and verify the photo-interpreted classification.

Targeted spot-checks of a short list of ambiguous features flagged during compilation: drive or walk to each specific location (a building of unclear use, a possibly gated private road, a name on a sign), photograph it, and record the resolved attribute.

roles.description: Make exact measurements and determine property boundaries. tasks.label: Direct or conduct surveys to establish legal boundaries for properties, based on legal deeds and titles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Suburban residential lot boundary survey (mortgage, fence, or addition permit): research the deed, recorded plat and adjoiner deeds; in the yard, hunt for existing corner monuments with a magnetic locator and shovel (buried rebar, pipes, nails in curbs), measure recovered evidence with RTK GNSS and a robotic total station, weigh occupation evidence (fences, hedges, driveways), resolve the boundary, drive new capped rebar at deficient corners, flag lines, and deliver a signed plat. Conditions: fenced yards, landscaping, pets, parked cars, homeowners asking questions.

Rural/large-acreage retracement (farm, ranch, timber tract): follow an old metes-and-bounds description across miles of brush, woods and creeks; search for stone corners, blazed/bearing trees, old fence corners and pipes; clear sightlines with a machete or chainsaw, run traverse/GNSS under canopy with obstructed sky, reconcile record calls with found evidence, set monuments and witness posts, and prepare the plat. Conditions: uneven terrain, mud, ticks, livestock, no site control.

Commercial ALTA/NSPS land title survey of a developed urban or suburban parcel: work from a title commitment and exception documents; recover street and block monuments in pavement and sidewalks amid traffic, locate buildings, parking, utilities and encroachments, plot easements, resolve the record boundary, set or reference corners, and certify the survey to lender and title company. Conditions: active parking lots, traffic control, pedestrians, tight schedule.

New subdivision/development: establish the parent tract boundary from the deed, then compute and stake lot corners and rights-of-way per the recorded plat on raw or graded land; recover controlling boundary monuments first, set permanent capped rebar and PK nails at final corners, and file the record of survey. Conditions: active construction site with earthmoving equipment, stripped ground, monuments destroyed and reset.

Disputed or evidence-poor boundary (conflicting deeds, sequential conveyances, overlaps/gaps, adverse-possession claims): extensive courthouse and archive research of chains of title, field interviews with neighbors, exhaustive search for ambiguous or contradictory monuments, professional judgment applying boundary law, a report or exhibit, and possible expert testimony; corners set only where the determination supports them.

It executes a supplied coordinate list; it does not research deeds, search for or recover existing boundary monuments, weigh conflicting evidence, or set permanent legal corner monuments.

Control for boundary or topographic mapping in rural, wooded or brushy terrain: reconnaissance through vegetation, driving monuments in soil, multi-hour static GNSS sessions or a total-station traverse under canopy where RTK is unreliable, ties to existing found monuments, post-processing and documentation.

Urban / roadway corridor control: setting PK nails, spikes or drilled marks in pavement and curb along a street or highway right-of-way, occupying points with GNSS in partly obstructed sky plus a total-station traverse and levels, working amid live traffic, parked cars and pedestrians.

Control network inside a large building or industrial facility for as-built scanning/BIM registration: establish floor marks and wall/column targets by total-station traverse and resection with no GNSS, level between floors, measure and document coordinates in the building frame.

High-order geodetic control or precise benchmarks (NGS-style): install a deep-driven rod or cast concrete monument with access cover, run multi-hour static GNSS sessions or precise differential leveling, submit to OPUS/network adjustment and prepare formal monument descriptions.

instances.label: Field check-and-adjust of a total station at a project site (construction site, roadway shoulder, rural boundary traverse): instrument set on a tripod, leveled, sighted on a well-defined target 50-200 m away; onboard routine run for horizontal collimation, vertical index, compensator/tilt and ATR; new correction values reviewed, accepted and stored, results logged. Weather, traffic and terrain are as found.

Two-peg (collimation) test and adjustment of an automatic or digital level, run in the job-site parking lot, a yard, or along the level line: staffs set at measured distances, readings taken from two instrument positions, collimation error computed, then either the electronic correction entered (digital level) or the reticle adjusting screw turned with a hex key while sighting through the eyepiece (optical level), and the test repeated to confirm.

Accessory and small-instrument adjustments in the shop or truck bay: tribrach optical plummet checked by rotating 180 degrees over a floor mark and nulled with grub screws, prism-pole and staff circular vials adjusted against a plumb line or jig, tripod heads tightened, prism constants verified. Mixed makes and models, hand tools from a drawer.

Periodic traceable verification and adjustment against known references at the firm's own check range: instrument mounted on forced-centering pillars or a calibrated EDM baseline, distances and angles compared to certified values per ISO 17123, stored scale/additive constants and collimation values updated, certificate/log written. Premises controlled by the employer.

Full service-center calibration and mechanical realignment of an instrument returned from the field: bench with collimators, housing opened, optics and EDM axis realigned, encoders and motors recalibrated, instrument re-certified. Performed by an in-house or manufacturer technician on a lab bench.

instances.label: Rural / large-tract boundary retracement: woods, brush, pasture or farmland. Research deed and plat, hunt for and dig out original monuments (iron pins, stones, fence corners) with a magnetic locator, occupy each found mark with RTK/static GNSS or a total station traverse under canopy, weigh conflicting physical evidence, set missing corners, and compute the tract's position, area and shape.

Developed / urban parcel or right-of-way boundary determination: subdivision lots, city blocks, roadway ROW. Recover cut crosses, pins and disks in pavement, curbs and yards, run a robotic-total-station traverse between GNSS-observed control points amid traffic, parked cars, fences and buildings, locate improvements, and resolve the parcel geometry for a boundary/ALTA plat.

Geodetic control network establishment and observation over a project area or county: recover or set control monuments, center and level tripods/fixed-height poles precisely over the marks, measure antenna heights, run multi-hour static GNSS sessions and ties to CORS/NGS marks, then adjust the network that fixes the tract's position and orientation. Roadside verges, open fields, rooftops.

Aerial determination of a large tract's position, extent, shape and topography: UAV photogrammetry or LiDAR with RTK/PPK over open land, a corridor, or a construction site; plan and fly the coverage grid, capture georeferenced imagery/point cloud, verify against checkpoints, and deliver the mapped limits, acreage and surface of the tract.

Survey of a tract inside an institution-controlled facility: open-pit mine, quarry, port terminal, industrial plant or utility-scale solar site with access control, maintained haul roads and an existing site control network. Determine working-area extents, pit/stockpile limits, and as-built positions and shapes of site features tied to that control.

instances.label: Wet-lab experimentation on biological samples in a university or company biomedical research lab, jointly with life scientists/chemists: cell and tissue culture, differentiation and treatment protocols, biochemical and molecular assays, staining and microscopy, iterating conditions across rounds until a result is obtained.

In-vivo animal studies with veterinarians and medical scientists in a vivarium/animal surgical suite: anesthesia and prep, surgical implantation of a device or creation of a model, physiological instrumentation and monitoring, post-op care, terminal tissue harvest.

Human-subject research sessions in a clinical research or gait/physiology lab with clinician collaborators: consenting and positioning participants, attaching markers, electrodes, wearables or probes, running exercise/imaging/recording protocols, logging data and de-instrumenting.

Designing, fabricating and commissioning custom research apparatus and prototypes to enable the experiments: machining/3D printing parts, microfabrication, assembling fluidics, sensors and electronics, wiring, calibrating and debugging the rig until it produces valid data.

Analysis, modeling and interpretation of the research data with collaborators: statistics, simulation, image/signal processing, protocol and study design, literature review, writing manuscripts and reports (no physical manipulation).

instances.label: R&D bench wet-lab follow-up on formulations/materials/reagents: after a first data set, the engineer specifies and runs the next round of variants (hydrogel/polymer formulations, coating chemistries, buffers, crosslinker levels), preparing solutions, weighing solids, running reactions/incubations, and quantifying results on plate readers, HPLC or rheometers in a standard lab.

Cell-culture / bioprocess process optimization: iterate media, feed, inducer, seeding density or differentiation parameters over successive runs of plates, shake flasks or mini-bioreactors to hit an established titer, viability or product-quality objective; requires sterile handling, incubators, sampling and assay readouts.

Specimen-level mechanical/materials follow-up testing of device components and prototypes: fabricate modified specimens (3D-printed scaffolds, polymer coupons, sutures, tubing), run tensile/fatigue/compression/toughness tests on a universal testing machine, and use the results to choose the next design or test matrix.

System-level bench verification of an assembled device with bespoke rigs: build or reconfigure a custom fixture, flow loop or instrumented test stand (catheter burst/fatigue rig, pump hemodynamic loop, sensor/electronics characterization bench, sterilization or package-integrity setup), route tubing and wiring, calibrate sensors, then run the follow-up test series and interpret it.

Pilot-plant or manufacturing process experiments in a cleanroom or on a production line: run a follow-up DOE on process parameters (molding, laser welding, coating, extrusion, fill-finish), produce sample lots, measure parts, and iterate to meet a process-capability objective.

Preclinical or human-facing follow-up study: an in vivo animal implantation or explant study, cadaver-lab test, or clinician usability session run in an animal facility, surgical suite or clinical space to close out a question raised by earlier data.

instances.label: Bench-scale screening/optimization campaign on a reaction or formulation step in a corporate or university R&D lab: weighing and dosing reagents/solvents into vials or small stirred reactors, running a designed set of conditions (temperature, catalyst loading, ratios), sampling for GC/HPLC, and iterating on the design of experiments. Standard labware, fume hoods, ambient pressure.

Reaction/catalyst performance testing on a lab reactor rig: loading catalyst into fixed-bed microreactors or an autoclave, leak-checking, running at elevated temperature and pressure with metered gas/liquid feeds for hours to weeks, with periodic sampling and online GC to build kinetic and deactivation data for scale-up.

Separation and solids-handling unit-operation studies on bespoke bench rigs: assembling/modifying glass or metal apparatus for distillation, extraction, crystallization, filtration, drying, or mixing; handling slurries, sticky solids and foaming; fixing leaks and plugging; cleaning fouled equipment between runs.

Analytical/characterization support for the studies: preparing, diluting, filtering and queuing samples; running HPLC/GC, titrations, particle size, viscosity, moisture; logging and reducing the data. Standard benchtop instruments in a controlled lab.

Pilot-plant campaign in the company's pilot hall: charging feedstocks from drums/hoppers, lining up valves and hoses, starting pumps and heaters, monitoring the DCS around the clock, drawing hourly process samples from sample ports, adjusting setpoints, shutting down, draining and cleaning out between runs.

Small-scale trial run outside the home lab: a skid-mounted or mobile test unit operated at a customer plant, refinery, biorefinery or field site with real (variable, dirty) feedstock, outdoors or in a shed, with local utility hookups and site-specific layout.

instances.label: First-article build of a prototype board in an in-house prototype lab or quick-turn assembly shop: solder paste applied to a bare PCB from the layout/BOM, dozens to hundreds of SMT parts (0402s, QFNs, BGAs, connectors) placed and reflowed, odd-form/through-hole parts and wires soldered, joints inspected before power-up.

Planned verification/characterization testing of the prototype: DUT powered from lab supplies or seated in a test fixture/socket, instruments (scope, logic analyzer, DMM, load, thermal chamber) connected to defined test points, a scripted test suite run over voltage and temperature, results logged and compared with the SPICE/thermal/signal-integrity simulation predictions.

Something is wrong — board won't boot, a rail sags, a high-speed link fails. Engineer probes arbitrary nets with scope and thermal camera, forms and tests hypotheses, cuts traces, tacks in bodge wires, piggybacks parts, retrofits shims/heatsinks, and iterates until root cause is found and the fix is proven on the hardware.

Directed component-level rework on an existing prototype board: swap a suspect or wrong-value part, reball and replace a BGA/FPGA, change passives to values chosen from a simulation sweep, then re-verify electrically.

System-level prototype integration in the lab: mount PCBs into a chassis or rack, install heatsinks with thermal interface material, drive dozens of screws, route and mate internal cables/FFCs and connectors, close the unit up, then run the system-level power/thermal/functional test.

No hardware involved: engineer builds or modifies a theoretical model of the product (SPICE, EM/signal-integrity, thermal FEA, or an architectural/RTL simulator), runs simulated tests, and revises the design — desk work at a workstation.

instances.label: Bring-up and debug of a new prototype board or first silicon at an engineering bench: apply power in stages, attach scope/logic-analyzer probes to unfamiliar test points, run ad-hoc firmware, chase unexpected failures, rework or strap the board, re-measure and document whether the design meets spec.

Design-verification/characterization campaign: DUT (chip on load board, or module in a fixture) presented to an automated tester, test suite swept across voltage/temperature/frequency corners over hours or overnight, results datalogged and compared to spec limits, margins and shmoo/pass-fail summaries produced.

Environmental, reliability and EMC qualification: DUT placed in a thermal/burn-in chamber or anechoic chamber, subjected to long thermal soaks, cycling, stress or emissions/immunity scans, with automated data acquisition and verification against the qualification spec.

Peripheral and interface verification: connector mating-cycle durability and insertion/withdrawal force, cable flex fatigue, port/display/touch or head-mounted-display performance and latency measurement; force, resistance and timing data recorded and checked against the interface specification.

Verification of assembled hardware in manufacturing: in-circuit/flying-probe and functional test of production boards on the line, checking each unit against the test spec, logging results and reviewing yield/test data to confirm the build meets requirements.

System/rack-level verification in the field: servers, storage and peripherals installed in a data center or customer integration hall are cabled, powered, link-checked and stress-tested; failures are swapped and retested, results recorded in the acceptance report.

Design validation / qualification testing in a lab: instrumenting a unit with thermocouples and probes, running it in a thermal chamber, EMC chamber, shock/vibe table or power/margining rig, monitoring behavior across corners, then modifying the hardware (heatsink, thermal interface, shielding, airflow ducting, cabling, component values) and re-running the profile to bring it into conformance.

Deployed fleet in a data center: telemetry flags a failed field-replaceable unit (disk/drive) in a standardized rack; the failed part is located and physically swapped so the system returns to spec.

Deployed fleet, complex issue: monitoring telemetry from installed servers/appliances and diagnosing an intermittent problem (thermal excursion, link/CRC errors, marginal power, firmware regression), then making the corrective modification on the machine — reseating/replacing DIMMs or cables, re-routing airflow, changing a mezzanine card, flashing corrected firmware — and verifying against spec.

Installed equipment at a field or customer site (industrial plant floor, telecom cabinet, vehicle/ship, remote or military installation): monitoring how the delivered hardware performs in situ and making on-site modifications — re-cabling, grounding/shielding fixes, board or module swaps, mounting changes — to bring it into conformance.

Ad-hoc micro-modification of an existing board to implement an engineering change: cut copper traces with a scalpel under a stereo microscope, tack 34-38 AWG jumper wires between pins/vias, piggyback resistors on existing parts, secure with epoxy — the exact cut and route decided at the bench from schematics.

Rack/server hardware integration and swaps in a lab rack room or data center: rack a chassis, install PCIe/NIC/GPU cards and drive trays, replace a module, run and dress power and network cabling to build a custom test configuration, then bring it up.

Fabricating custom cables/harnesses to a special spec: cut, strip, crimp, insert contacts into connector housings and label wires (often a batch of one or a few) for a custom instrument, backplane or test setup, then continuity-test them.

Mechanical modification of existing equipment: machining cutouts, drilling and tapping holes in an enclosure or mounting plate for new connectors/fans, fabricating brackets and thermal mounts — usually in a lab/workshop, occasionally as a retrofit at a customer or field installation site.

instances.label: Construction-administration walkdown / punch-list of a newly completed electrical installation in a commercial, institutional or industrial building: engineer walks an active, cluttered jobsite with drawings and specs, opens panelboards and enclosures, verifies feeder sizes, breaker ratings, grounding/bonding, terminations, labeling, working clearances, device locations and penetrations against the approved design and NEC, and writes a deficiency list for the contractor.

Commissioning / acceptance witnessing of major electrical equipment at a substation, data center, hospital or plant: engineer witnesses insulation-resistance, CT ratio, protective-relay and functional trip tests on switchgear, transformers, UPS and generators, checks as-built wiring against schematics and relay setting sheets, verifies interlocks and labeling, and signs off on energization.

Routine observation of operations in an operating, owner-controlled facility (plant, substation/converter station, data center): engineer walks the floor/yard on a fixed route observing energized equipment, taking infrared and visual readings of MCCs, cabinets, transformers and buses, reading gauges and indicators, listening for abnormal noise, and flagging hot spots, leaks and safety non-conformances.

In-plant conformance inspection of manufactured electrical assemblies against engineering specification: PCB assemblies, control panels and harnesses checked on the production floor or in a test area for correct components, placement, polarity, solder/termination quality and dimensional conformance, plus functional electrical test before release.

Field survey of dispersed outdoor assets: thermographic and visual inspection of a utility-scale PV array, wind-farm collection system, or overhead distribution/transmission line for defective modules/strings, hot connections, damaged hardware and standards compliance, over open terrain and in variable weather.

Inspection of installations at occupied residential or small-commercial premises taken as found: service upgrade, EV charger, backup generator or tenant fit-out; engineer inspects the panel and feeders in a basement/closet, verifies the work matches the submitted design and code, and investigates a customer complaint about voltage or nuisance tripping.

instances.label: Bench prototype integration in the employer's engineering lab: the specialist cables a fixed UHF reader to two to four antennas via coax, mounts them on a test frame, powers the reader over PoE, loads firmware/SDK, applies sample tags to product samples, sets power/session/filter parameters, and iterates until read rates and cross-read behavior meet the design spec.

On-site pilot/production integration at a customer distribution center or plant: mount reader enclosure and antennas on a dock-door or conveyor portal, run coax and Ethernet/PoE, tie in light stacks or PLC I/O, tag sample cases/pallets, tune power and filtering to suppress stray reads from adjacent doors, and validate reads against the WMS before sign-off.

Software-side integration performed at a desk: configuring edge/middleware (e.g., reader management and event-filtering software), mapping tag-read events to ERP/WMS transactions through APIs, writing or adapting glue code, and testing against simulated or captured read streams. No hardware is handled.

Tag selection and placement engineering in a lab or test chamber: evaluate candidate inlays on the actual substrate (metal parts, liquid-filled bottles, cartons), affix tags at several candidate positions on sample items, measure read range/orientation sensitivity with test equipment, and specify the tag model and placement for the design.

Embedding RFID hardware into a product or asset design: integrating a reader or tag module into a PCB/enclosure, antenna impedance matching with a VNA, hand-assembling and reworking a prototype, then bench-testing the integrated unit against requirements.

Integration testing of the RFID data path into WMS/ERP/inventory applications: verifying EPC-to-item mapping, read filtering and deduplication, event triggers, database records, exception handling and reports, using staged or captured read data at a workstation.

On-site pilot/user-acceptance testing of the deployed software at a customer distribution center, store, or hospital: running scripted read cycles through portal or handheld software, comparing captured counts against expected inventory, tuning configuration parameters, and documenting pass/fail results for sign-off.

Testing handheld/mobile RFID applications and sled interfaces: verifying scan sessions, UI workflows, cycle-count logic, offline caching and back-end synchronization of the app, then logging defects for the developers.

Post-change verification after software patches, middleware upgrades, or reader firmware updates: smoke tests of interfaces and APIs, security/compliance checks, verification that prior defects are resolved, and release documentation.

instances.label: Distribution center / 3PL warehouse survey for supply-chain RFID: walk receiving, shipping and dock-door areas with a floor plan; take RF noise-floor/spectrum readings at candidate portal locations; temporarily rig reader antennas and run test reads of tagged cases/pallets driven through by forklift; inspect racking, metal, ceiling mounting points, conduit, power and network drops; observe and time the receiving/shipping workflow and interview supervisors; deliver reader/antenna placement configuration, impacted processes and obstacle list.

Manufacturing plant survey for WIP/tool tracking: assess RF-hostile conditions (metal work-in-process, welders, VFDs, motors, existing 900 MHz/Wi-Fi systems), measure interference near production lines and fenced automation cells, evaluate where tags can be applied to parts and where readers can mount on conveyors or gantries without disrupting line operation, and document process changes and mounting/safety obstacles.

Retail store survey (apparel or grocery, sales floor plus backroom): map fixtures, shelving, stockroom shelving depth, checkout and exit zones; test handheld/overhead reader read zones and cross-reads through walls; note liquids/metal product effects, customer traffic constraints, aesthetics and mounting limits; recommend fixed-reader vs. handheld/robot configuration and cycle-count process changes.

Hospital, clinic or lab survey for asset/specimen tracking: walk corridors, supply rooms, ORs and equipment storage with escorts; check EMI-sensitive equipment and existing RTLS/Wi-Fi, ceiling type and mounting rights, infection-control and access restrictions; determine reader/exciter placement, tag types for sterile equipment, and how clinical workflows would be affected.

Outdoor or semi-outdoor site survey: trailer yard gates, port/intermodal lanes, construction laydown yards or oilfield pipe yards. Assess vehicle speeds and lane geometry, weather exposure, enclosure and power availability, existing gate infrastructure, GPS/RF interference, and mud/dust; determine gate portal configuration and civil-works obstacles.

Smaller or specialized sites: library, records/file room, office IT asset tracking, event venue, or a follow-up re-survey after a layout change. Short walkthrough, floor-plan verification, spot read tests, stakeholder interviews, and a written configuration/obstacle memo.

tasks.label: Perform acceptance testing on newly installed or updated systems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Distribution center / warehouse: acceptance test of newly installed dock-door RFID portals. Engineer runs known tagged pallets and mixed cases through each portal on a forklift/pallet jack at varied speeds, orientations and load densities, compares reads to the expected tag manifest, checks for stray/cross reads from adjacent doors and directionality, confirms events reach the middleware/WMS, adjusts power/antenna aim as needed, and documents pass/fail against the contracted read-rate criteria (e.g., >99%).

Retail store (apparel/grocery) item-level RFID go-live: verify overhead/fixed readers at fitting rooms, exits and POS plus handheld/rolling reader coverage across sales floor and stockroom, run a controlled known-tag audit to compute read accuracy and false-read rate, check for reads bleeding into adjacent zones, verify counts flow to the inventory platform, and write the acceptance report.

Manufacturing / packaging line: acceptance test of a newly installed or upgraded RFID tunnel, conveyor read point, or print-and-apply encoder. Run product at full line speed, verify 100% encode/verify and read of every case, confirm photo-eye/PLC triggers and reject handshake, check shielding and neighboring-line interference, tune and re-run, and sign off with a documented test run.

Hospital / clinical or lab facility: acceptance test of a newly installed RFID/RTLS asset- or specimen-tracking system. Walk reference-tagged assets through doorways, rooms, corridors and elevators, check room-level location accuracy and event latency, verify alerting and integration with the asset system, confirm no interference with medical equipment, and document results with facilities/biomed staff.

Outdoor gate/yard at a port, terminal or truck yard: acceptance test of a newly installed vehicle/container RFID gate. Drive tagged trucks and trailers through the lane at operating speed in real weather, verify reads across tag mounting positions and lanes, check no cross-lane reads, verify gate/camera/OCR triggers and data to the yard system, and document.

Post-update verification after a middleware, reader-firmware or WMS-integration upgrade: mostly desk-based regression checks of configurations, data flows and reports, combined with a short physical smoke test at a few read points using a handful of known tags before returning the system to production.

instances.label: Install a fixed RFID read portal at distribution-center dock doors: locate and mount antenna brackets/frames to door frames or overhead steel, run and terminate coax/PoE cable in conduit or tray, mount and power the reader, tie into the network, mount motion sensors/light stacks, and bring the portal up. Work on ladders/lifts around active dock traffic.

Install or expand RFID infrastructure in a retail store, hospital, or office: mount ceiling-grid or overhead readers and antennas, pull cable above ceiling tiles, install handheld charging cradles and door/exit readers, cable to IDF, configure and verify reads, all in an occupied facility during off-hours.

Post-install commissioning: RF site survey with spectrum analyzer, walking or driving tagged cases/pallets through the portal, measuring read rates and stray reads, physically re-aiming antennas and adjusting power/polarization, re-testing, and documenting results for customer acceptance.

Maintain/troubleshoot a deployed system on a customer site: diagnose a dead or degraded reader, antenna, or cable run, swap hardware, re-terminate or reroute damaged coax (often forklift-damaged), replace GPIO sensors, reflash and re-verify, in a live warehouse/plant/store.

Bench/lab work: characterize tag and inlay RF performance (sensitivity, read range, orientation), qualify reader and antenna samples, encode and verify sample tags for a customer program, in a company test lab or anechoic chamber.

Integrate RFID into a manufacturing or conveyor line: mount readers/antennas and shielding on the conveyor or workcell, wire I/O to the PLC, tune trigger timing and read zones, validate against production throughput on the plant floor.

tasks.label: Test tags or labels to ensure readability.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench/lab characterization of candidate tag samples before selection: the specialist attaches sample inlays/labels to representative substrates or products, runs threshold-power, read-range and orientation-sensitivity sweeps on lab measurement gear (benchtop chamber or anechoic chamber), compares to category limits (e.g., ARC-style), and records pass/fail per tag model. Setting: an RFID lab or engineering test bench inside a company facility.

Quality check of encoded/printed RFID labels and inlay rolls before use: verify each label encodes and reads back correctly, spot-check rolls for dead or weak tags, screen out failures, and log yield. Setting: a label converting line, a print-and-encode station, or a distribution-center labeling room.

Read-rate verification of tagged cases/pallets through a fixed read zone in a distribution center: run tagged cartons repeatedly through a dock-door portal, conveyor tunnel, or pack-out station, measure percentage of tags read, identify unread items and shadowed tags, and report against an acceptance criterion (e.g., >99%). Setting: warehouse/DC floor with standard racking, conveyors and dock doors.

In-situ sweep of an operating floor to confirm applied tags read: walk (or drive) the sales floor, stockroom, warehouse aisles or clinical storeroom interrogating every tagged item, compare reads to expected item list, and flag items whose tags did not respond. Setting: retail sales floor, warehouse aisles, or hospital supply area, during or after operating hours.

Field testing of tags on difficult assets and materials: on-metal tags on tools, machinery, cylinders, returnable containers or vehicles; tags near liquids; assets in laydown yards, job sites or customer premises. The specialist mounts tags in trial positions, reads at varying distances/orientations with a handheld or field kit, and decides an acceptable tag and placement. Setting: as-found outdoor yards, job sites and customer facilities.

instances.label: Environmental compliance inspection/audit of an industrial facility (manufacturing plant, metal finisher, chemical plant) under air/water/RCRA permits: walk process areas and hazardous-waste accumulation areas, check container labeling and accumulation dates, secondary containment, spill kits, control-device operation, look for leaks/spills, photograph findings, review permit and monitoring records, interview operators, then issue a written compliance findings report with deficiencies and corrective actions.

Evaluation of a municipal wastewater or drinking-water treatment plant's operational effectiveness: walk headworks, clarifiers, aeration basins, digesters, filters and disinfection; check equipment condition and process indicators; collect or oversee effluent samples; review operating logs, SCADA trends and DMR data against permit limits; report performance findings and optimization recommendations.

Routine scheduled surveillance round of a plant's process and pollution-control equipment (scrubber, baghouse, thermal oxidizer, flare, pumps, tanks) inside an industrial or municipal facility: traverse a fixed route on walkways and stairs, log gauge/instrument readings, capture thermal and acoustic data, sniff for gas leaks, note spills, debris or corrosion, and file the dated inspection record with flagged anomalies.

Quarterly landfill surface emissions monitoring (SEM) compliance survey under NSPS/EG: traverse the landfill surface on a serpentine pattern at ~30 m spacing with a methane detector, record concentrations and GPS locations, identify exceedances above 500 ppm for remonitoring/repair, and produce the compliance monitoring record.

Site inspection at a construction site, remediation site or industrial yard: walk uneven, muddy terrain around active equipment to assess erosion and sediment controls, stormwater BMPs, stockpile covers, dewatering discharges, drum/soil staging and excavation practices; direct contractor corrective actions and complete the SWPPP/site inspection form.

Program inspection/audit at a municipal agency or utility (e.g., MS4 stormwater program, pretreatment program, spill-prevention program): review SOPs, permits, monitoring records and training files at the agency office, interview staff, and conduct on-site verification visits to outfalls, yards or facilities before writing a program effectiveness evaluation.

Preparing or reviewing the QA and safety documentation for the inspection: sampling and analysis plan, quality assurance project plan, chain-of-custody procedures, data quality objectives, and the site health-and-safety / safety-inspection protocol (PPE, H2S and benzene monitoring, confined-space and lockout rules); includes staging and calibrating field instruments and assembling bottle/preservative kits and coolers before the trip.

On-site sampling support during the inspection at the complex facility: collecting effluent and process-wastewater grab samples at sample ports and outfalls, sludge/waste samples from tanks, drums or roll-offs, occasional soil or stormwater samples; filling and preserving bottles, labeling, decontaminating equipment between points, collecting QC duplicates and blanks, completing chain-of-custody forms and icing coolers for shipment.

Field screening and monitoring rounds during the inspection: walking defined routes through process units and tank farms taking instrument readings (optical gas imaging / IR camera for leaks, PID or LEL meter, opacity, gauge, level and temperature readings), thermal imaging of equipment, and photo-documenting equipment condition and monitoring points for the inspection record.

Adaptive compliance walkthrough alongside the inspectors at a facility the team may be visiting for the first time: observing operating practices and control-equipment performance, checking hazardous-waste container labeling, secondary containment and housekeeping, judging on the fly which units, discharge points or records warrant closer attention, and questioning operators and EHS staff about process changes.

Post-inspection quality assurance and reporting: validating the laboratory data package against the QAPP, checking chain-of-custody completeness, holding times, blanks and duplicate recoveries, reconciling field notes and photos, and drafting the technical/engineering sections of the inspection report and recommended follow-up. roles.description: Promote worksite or product safety by applying knowledge of industrial processes, mechanics, chemistry, psychology, and industrial health and safety laws. Includes industrial product safety engineers.

tasks.label: Investigate industrial accidents, injuries, or occupational diseases to determine causes and preventive measures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Machine-related injury on a manufacturing floor (amputation, crush, laceration): safety engineer secures/inspects the machine, examines guarding and interlocks, tests lockout-tagout, photographs and measures the point of operation, interviews the injured worker and witnesses, reviews maintenance and training records, determines root cause and writes corrective/preventive actions.

Minor injury or near-miss in a plant or warehouse (slip/trip/fall, strain, hand cut, forklift near-miss): quick site walk-down within hours, photos of the location and equipment, short interviews, review of the job procedure, 5-why/root-cause write-up and countermeasure recommendation.

Occupational illness / exposure case (noise-induced hearing loss, dermatitis, respiratory complaint, chemical over-exposure): reconstruct the exposure by walking the process, taking air or noise measurements with sampling pumps and dosimeters on workers, checking ventilation and PPE use, reviewing SDSs and medical/exposure records, and concluding on cause and controls.

Serious or catastrophic event (fire, explosion, chemical release, fatality) inside a facility: scene is damaged, debris-strewn, possibly still hazardous; engineer works a preserved scene with OSHA/insurers, sequences physical evidence, collects samples and failed components, coordinates lab analysis, and produces a multi-week causal analysis.

Incident at a construction, utility, or other field site (contractor fall, trench collapse, mobile-equipment struck-by): layout differs site to site, weather and terrain uncontrolled, equipment unfamiliar; engineer travels out, documents the scene, interviews crew and subcontractors, and determines cause and preventive measures.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: routine data-capture inspection rounds in an industrial facility. It transfers only to the scene-documentation portion of an accident investigation (navigating a plant and capturing images/thermal data at defined points); it does not cover interviewing witnesses, disassembling or functionally testing the involved machine, or reasoning to a root cause and corrective actions, which are the output the employer accepts.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: accident-scene documentation for reconstruction. The autonomous element is limited to flight-path planning and imagery capture with an operator on scene; the causal analysis, evidence handling and preventive-measure determination that define this task are still performed by human investigators.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous hazard monitoring in a process plant. Shows a robot can traverse an institution-controlled industrial site and flag anomalies, but flagging an abnormal condition is not investigating an injury or illness to determine its cause and the preventive measures required.

instances.label: Airborne chemical/dust exposure assessment at a manufacturing or chemical plant: select representative employees and tasks, calibrate personal sampling pumps, clip pumps on workers with sorbent tubes/filter cassettes in the breathing zone for a full shift, run parallel area samples, retrieve and cap media, complete chain-of-custody to an accredited lab, compare results with OSHA PELs and document.

Occupational noise survey at a production facility: walk the floor with a calibrated Type 2 sound level meter taking readings at machines and operator positions to build a noise map, fit noise dosimeters on selected workers for a shift, download and compute TWA/dose against the OSHA 1910.95 action level and PEL, and document hearing-conservation coverage.

Routine area atmospheric/gas monitoring and leak-emission compliance rounds at an industrial facility (refinery, midstream plant, chemical works, utility, wastewater): fixed-route direct-reading measurements of combustible/toxic gas, oxygen and vapor concentrations plus fugitive-emission leak surveys, logging readings and flagging exceedances for the compliance record.

Radiological survey at a nuclear plant, national lab, medical or industrial-radiography facility: dose-rate mapping along defined survey routes, scanning surfaces/vehicles for contamination with alpha-beta and gamma detectors, comparing to posting and regulatory limits and recording the survey map.

Routine indoor environmental quality and thermal monitoring rounds in an institution-controlled building (offices, school, hospital wing): scheduled multi-room readings of CO2, temperature, relative humidity, CO and particulates against ASHRAE/agency guidance, producing a periodic compliance/monitoring report.

Non-routine, as-found field testing: pre-entry confined-space atmospheric clearance (O2/LEL/H2S at a tank, vault or manhole) before a permit entry, heat-stress WBGT monitoring on an outdoor crew, silica/welding-fume and noise spot checks on an active construction or field site, and complaint-driven indoor air quality investigations where the source must be traced.
